title: Batch jitter & KV-shadow experiment check-in
content:
Date: 2026-06-15
Attendees: Aisha K (owner), Marco C, Lina R, Priya N, Tomás A, (ops: CI stub)
Meeting length: 35m
Goal: Quick sync on the batch jitter source (spikes around small-chat workloads) and the KV-shadow experiment that ran last week comparing eviction strategies under mixed sequences.

TL;DR:
- We saw an intermittent +2.1–3.5% 95th percentile latency bump on small-request workloads during peak when batch wait jitter was enabled (experiment variant with jitter=3–10ms).
- KV-shadow (shadowing cache reads/writes to a secondary policy) shows a ~7% higher hit-rate with the freq-decay variant but introduced a small increase in write amplification; no customer-visible regressions in correctness observed.
- Next steps: tighten the jitter distribution, add a short-circuit path for <64-token requests, and run a 48h canary with the freq-decay policy in shadow->staging route.

Observations / Data points:
- Workload: mixed chat traces (80% short-turn <64 tokens, 20% long-turn >256 tokens). Run in prod-shadow and staging main traffic capture.
- Latency delta: baseline (no jitter) p95 = 78ms. jitter-enabled p95 median of experiment windows = 80.6ms; spike windows up to 82.5ms. CPU/GPU utilization unchanged.
- When we enable jitter with coalescing window >4ms, small requests frequently miss the head of a batch and end up in tiny single-item microbatches; this increases queue overhead and RPC count by ~4%.
- KV-shadow results (24h): LRU baseline miss rate 12.9%, freq-decay miss rate 11.9% (absolute improvement 1.0pp, relative ~7.8%). Write amplification (writes to secondary shadow) increased 3.2% due to more metadata churn under freq-decay.

Experiment config (for reproducibility):
- Batch jitter variants: uniform jitter U(0,3ms), U(0,6ms), U(3,10ms) applied at request entrance to coalescer. Coalescing window base=8ms.
- KV-shadow: primary (LRU) + shadow writer that records reads/writes to a freq-decay policy sampler; eviction budget limited to 10% of main cache size.
- Traces: 72h rolling capture of canary traffic, anonymized.

Hypotheses: 
1) The p95 bump is caused by jitter pushing many small requests off the batch boundary and onto single-item handling paths; the combination of jitter and coalescer granularity creates microbatch fragmentation.
2) freq-decay improves hit-rate by retaining hot sequences longer, which is helpful for customer chat patterns with repeated short-turn tokens. The extra write amplification is an engineering cost but likely acceptable for Dedicated customers with higher cache sizes.

Decisions made in meeting:
- Roll jitter back to U(0,3ms) on the global canary to reduce fragmentation and continue experiments with shorter windows. (Owner: Aisha, ETA: 48h)
- Implement a fast-path for requests with input_tokens < 64 that bypasses the coalescer if current batch size==0 and queue depth < 2; this reduces head-of-line latency for small chats. (Owner: Marco, ETA: 1 sprint)
- Schedule a 48h staging canary that applies freq-decay policy in read-shadow mode (no live writes) to collect longer-term hit-rate and memory churn metrics. If stable, move to write-shadow for a second 48h run. (Owner: Lina, ETA: staging run starts 2026-06-20)
- Add tracing tag batch.fragmentation=true when request leaves coalescer as single-item batch for easier aggregation. (Owner: Priya, ETA: adenine patch by 2026-06-17)

Action items / Owners:
- Aisha: Rollback global jitter to U(0,3ms), coordinate with rollout-service and ops to monitor p95. Watchlist: traces with tag batch.fragmentation=true. (Due: 2026-06-17)
- Marco: Implement small-request fast-path, write unit+integration tests, land in canary runtime image. (Due: 2026-06-29)
- Lina: Stand up 48h staging canary for freq-decay read-shadow; capture evictions, hit-rate, memory-pressure charts. (Due: start 2026-06-20)
- Priya: Add tracing tag to coalescer and wire up a lightweight dashboard tile showing microbatch counts per minute per host. (Due: 2026-06-17)
- Tomás: Run a short thermals check (GPU/CPU power draw) during the next staging run and confirm no thermal throttling correlation. (Due: 2026-06-18)

Risks / Open questions:
- Write amplification from freq-decay in full write-shadow mode could increase SSD wear in smaller Dedicated nodes; need to model cost for 3-year P50 node lifecycle. (Finance/ops ask: estimate added GB writes/day before moving to write-shadow)
- Small-request fast-path complexity: does bypassing coalescer break any fairness or request-priority invariants? Need SRE review.
- Jitter testing coverage: current load tests don't exercise the exact short-turn-heavy mix seen in a subset of customers—need synthetic load generator tweak.

Notes from quick debugging session after standup:
- Trace 2026-06-14T17:05 UTC: single tiny batch (size=1) where request waited 9ms before dispatch because jitter pushed it past a boundary; handler added 1.2ms overhead when falling through to micro-path.
- Suggested immediate mitigations: reduce max jitter, revert coalescer to always emit after floor(2ms) if queue_depth>3. We took the reduce-max-jitter path for now.

Meeting appendix (raw links):
- Perf dashboard: internal-dashboard/serving/runtime/batching/p95
- Trace capture: internal-dashboard/trace/trace-2026-06-15
- PR (fast-path prototype): github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/482

Quick retrospective: the shadow approach is paying off — we can see small but meaningful hit-rate improvements without risking correctness. However, small-request behavior remains fragile when we try to tune batching to reduce average latency; microbatch fragmentation is the core tradeoff. Our plan balances a fast-path for tiny requests plus conservative jitter and continuing shadow evaluation for cache policy.

If you want to step into the data, ping Lina for the raw exported CSVs (she has the sample IDs and anonymized user traces).

Next sync: ad-hoc check-in when staging canary starts (2026-06-20) or weekly standup slot (Thursday 10:30 PT).
